newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Airlines profits hit by soaring fuel costs.
newsitem.headline: Airlines profits hit by soaring fuel costs.

text.p: World airlines appear headed for their second consecutive year of record profits, but soaring fuel costs are slicing into their overall revenues, the head of the industry's global body said Monday.

International Air Transport Association Director-General Pierre Jeanniot warned executives from over 250 member companies that a rush by carriers into hasty alliances to capture a bigger chunk of the booming market could bring more problems than successes.
"This year should deliver another record profit ... With interest charges slightly decreased, we would be looking at a net result of $5.5 billion," Jeanniot told the annual general meeting of IATA.
But that figure would be well down on the $6 billion he forecast in April this year before jet fuel price rises began seriously hitting the airlines. Fuel accounts for 11 percent of airline costs.

IATA airlines, which include highly profitable companies as well as chronic money-losers, are fighting to fill the $15.6 billion hole left in their coffers by the recession of the early 1990s and the Gulf Crisis of 1990-91.
In 1994 and 1995, overall revenues began to climb and in 1995 reached $5.2 billion -- partly due to the industry surge in Asia and the Pacific.
Jeanniot said that last year's results were underpinned by 8.2 percent growth in passenger and cargo traffic.

But the climb back into profitability after the most disastrous period for the airlines since the Geneva- and Montreal-based IATA was founded in 1945 was largely achieved through unit cost reductions, Jeanniot said.

"Airlines have downsized, outsourced, concentrated on core business ... We could be reaching a point of diminishing returns in our ability to deliver further significant reductions in unit cost," the former Air Canada chief said.

"And their are various things that can divert us from our prifitable flight path, such as infrastructure charges, which are outside our control," he said, referring to mounting levies by airports and governments for services.

Jeanniot said a key concern was fuel. Airlines paid an average world-wide price last year of 65.2 U.S. cents a gallon. But that soared to 77.5 cents in September after the United States fired Cruise missiles against Iraq.

"Now I don't know how much it costs to build and deliver a Cruise missile, but, taken over a year, the extra fuel cost incurred by IATA carriers on their international scheduled services would amount to $832 million," Jeanniot said.
"If pressing a firing button can dramatically increase airlines costs, it also points up the sheer fragility of their hard-won profitability."
Many European airlines have announced they are raising prices because of fuel costs, and IATA has called an emergency meeting in Geneva next week to discuss a concerted response by its members.
